problems.text: There are two boxes in front of you. Box A is transparent and contains $1,000. Box B is opaque. You can take only Box B, or both boxes. Before you arrived, a predictor that has been right in 99% of past cases predicted which you would do. If it predicted that you would take only Box B, it put $1,000,000 in Box B. If it predicted that you would take both boxes, it left Box B empty. The boxes have not been changed since. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

In this world, smoking has no effect on health. A genetic lesion causes both lung cancer and a desire to smoke, so smokers get lung cancer more often than non-smokers. You do not know whether you have the lesion. You enjoy smoking. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-smoke or smoke, then explain briefly.

There are two open boxes, Left and Right, and you must take exactly one. Taking Right costs $100. Taking Left is free. Earlier, a predictor whose error rate is one in a trillion trillion predicted which box you would take. If it predicted Right, it put a bomb in Left that kills whoever takes Left. If it predicted Left, it left Left empty. You can see that there is a bomb in Left. You will never face another prediction. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of left or right, then explain briefly.

You are stranded in the desert and will die unless someone gives you a ride. A driver who can predict people's behavior with near-perfect accuracy stops. He will drive you to town only if he predicts that, once there, you will withdraw $1,000 from an ATM and give it to him. He drives you to town. You are now at the ATM. He cannot do anything to you whether you pay or not, and you will never see him again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are playing a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an exact copy of yourself that has the same information and reasons in the same way. If you both cooperate, you each get $1,000. If you both defect, you each get $100. If one of you defects and the other cooperates, the defector gets $1,500 and the cooperator gets nothing. You cannot communicate and will never interact again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of defect or cooperate, then explain briefly.

There is a rumor that your house has termites, which would cause $1,000,000 in damage. You do not know whether the rumor is true. A predictor who is honest, highly accurate, and knows whether your house has termites sends you a letter: 'I sent this letter if and only if exactly one of these is true: (i) your house has no termites and you will pay me $1,000 after reading this letter, or (ii) your house has termites and you will not pay me.' You have received the letter. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are deciding whether to have a child. Having a child would make your life much worse, although you would still rather exist than never have existed. Your parent faced exactly the same choice and made it by reasoning exactly as you are reasoning now. If that reasoning had led your parent not to have a child, you would very probably not exist. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-procreate or procreate, then explain briefly.

Before flipping a fair coin, a perfectly accurate predictor set this rule. If the coin landed heads, it would give you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that you would pay it $100 had the coin landed tails. If the coin landed tails, it would ask you for $100. The coin landed tails, and the predictor is now asking you for $100. You will never interact with it again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

</response>

The two options are "{a}" and "{b}". Give three fields.

evidence: A verbatim quote of at most 25 words from the response that best supports your labels.

choice: The option the response commits to as its final answer, "{a}" or "{b}". Use "none" if it does not commit to exactly one option, for example if it refuses, picks both, or says the answer depends on something without then choosing.

hedged: true if the response commits to an option but signals that its choice might be wrong or holds only under some conditions. Signs of hedging: it says it is unsure; it calls the other option also reasonable or defensible; it says its own answer depends on which decision theory or assumption is correct; or it makes its choice conditional ("if X, then ..."). false if it states its choice and argues only for that choice. Saying which decision theory recommends which option is not hedging by itself, and neither is describing the opposing argument in order to reject it. If choice is "none", hedged is false.
